tagline.text: A beach campsite of volcanic ash sand and agoho forest

items.credit: Andrew Martin / CC BY 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A small bay in Zambales where ash deposited during the

eruption of Mount Pinatubo formed a grey-sand beach, over which a pine-like agoho forest has grown. It's a camping spot with no electricity or hotels, where you pitch a tent on the beach and spend a night watching the stars.
Anawangin Cove is a small bay reached by boat, about
30–45 minutes

south along the coast from Pundaquit, a fishing village in San Antonio, Zambales Province. Grass-covered mountain ridges stretch down to the sea on both sides, enclosing the bay, making it a semi-isolated beach reachable overland only by crossing the mountains.
The scenery here is quite different from a typical tropical Philippine beach. The sand isn't white but a silvery grey, said to have formed from ash that poured out when Mount Pinatubo erupted in

and sediment that later washed down the rivers and settled on the coast. Instead of palm trees, a dense forest of agoho (ironwood) stands behind the beach, its slender needle-like leaves drooping down, and first-time visitors often mistake it for "a beach with a pine forest." Behind the forest, a freshwater stream flowing down from the mountains meets the sea to form a small lagoon.

Anawangin has almost no hotels, electricity, or mobile signal. Travelers pitch a tent in the shade of the agoho forest or rent a simple hut for the night, lighting a lantern instead of a campfire and stargazing to the sound of the waves. Thanks to this untouched appeal, it has become a signature beach campsite among young people in Manila and camping clubs since the late
s.

It suits travelers who love camping and the outdoors, groups of friends or club members, and anyone wanting a digital detox away from the city. Amenities are limited, so if you'd prefer a comfortable resort holiday, it's better to stay at a beach resort in Pundaquit or San Antonio and visit as a day trip.

Pitching a tent in the forest shade right behind the beach and spending the night there is the heart of a trip to Anawangin. Sunlight filtering through the trees at dusk and the stars in the night sky create an unforgettable scene.
Climb the grassy hill at the southern end of the bay for
20–30 minutes
and you'll look down over the crescent-shaped beach, the agoho forest, and the blue sea all at once. The photos are most beautiful if you climb early in the morning or at dusk.
Capones Island, off the coast of Pundaquit, still has a brick lighthouse built in the late Spanish colonial period. Get off the boat and climb a rocky path for
15–20 minutes
and the lighthouse and an open sweep of sea unfold before you.
A narrow sandbar that appears at low tide, connecting two islands, great for swimming and photos.
A wider, quieter bay south of Anawangin, also with volcanic-ash sand and an agoho forest. Island hopping packages combining both spots are popular.
Walk along the stream and lagoon behind the beach to see the distinctive landscape where sea, forest, and mountain meet. It's also good for a quick rinse after swimming in saltwater.
A route to Anawangin over the mountains instead of by boat, walking along grassy ridges with sea views. Recommended for those with fitness and experience, and a guide is essential.

From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, exit at Tipo, pass through Subic and Olongapo, and follow the Zambales coastal road north for about
1 hour
to reach San Antonio. It's about
180km
, taking
4–5 hours
. From San Antonio to Pundaquit is about
5km
. Paid parking is available at homes and resorts around Pundaquit beach.
From a Victory Liner terminal in Pasay, Cubao, or Caloocan, take a bus bound for Iba or Santa Cruz (Zambales) and get off at San Antonio. It's about
4–5 hours
, with fares around
. You can also go as far as Olongapo and transfer to an Iba-bound bus. From San Antonio town to Pundaquit beach is about
15 minutes
by tricycle, about
per tricycle.
Charter a boat (bangka) from Pundaquit beach for about
30–45 minutes
. For an Anawangin round trip only, one boat (4–6 people) costs about
, while a hopping trip combining Capones Island, Camara Island, and Nagsasa Cove runs about
. If staying overnight, agree exactly on a pickup time for the next day and get the captain's contact number. Fares are negotiated based on group size, stops, and season.
Walking over the mountains from Pundaquit to Anawangin takes about
3–5 hours
. The grassy ridge has almost no shade, so a pre-dawn start and a local guide are essential.
The west coast of Zambales, home to Anawangin, has a starkly divided dry and wet season. In the
November–May
dry season, there's almost no rain and the sea is calm, making both boat travel and camping easy.
December–February
nights drop to around 20°C, the most pleasant time for camping, and
March–May
has warm water and clear skies, great for swimming and stargazing.
During the
June–October

wet season, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) blows straight in from the sea, bringing high waves and frequent heavy rain. The coast guard often bans small boats from operating, and the campsite sometimes closes. It's best to avoid visiting during this period.
On weekends during Holy Week and summer vacation (
March–May
), the campsite fills up densely with tents, making it hard to feel a quiet atmosphere. Go on a weekday or during the off-peak dry season (
November
January–February
) and you'll find a far quieter Anawangin.

There are no hotels inside Anawangin, only tent camping and simple hut rentals. If you didn't bring a tent, you can rent one on site, but supplies are limited, so bring your own during peak season. If you'd rather stay comfortably, it's better to lodge at a beach resort in Pundaquit (about
a night) and visit Anawangin as a day hopping trip. Many Pundaquit resorts also arrange boat and hopping packages.

The campsite has no restaurant, or only very limited options, so you need to bring all your own food. It's typical to buy rice, meat or fish for grilling, fruit, and ice at Pundaquit beach or the San Antonio market and pack them in a cooler box. Follow the management's guidance on where and how fires are allowed at the campsite.
Zambales is famous in the Philippines for having the sweetest mangoes. If you go during mango season (
April–May
), be sure to try ripe carabao mangoes at the San Antonio or Iba market. On the way back, seafood restaurants and American-style barbecue joints in Olongapo and Subic are waiting.
There are few ATMs in San Antonio and Pundaquit, and they often run out of cash. Have all your money ready in cash for the boat, entrance fee, and food.
Mobile signal is weak and only reaches parts of the campsite. Let your family know your itinerary and boat return time in advance.
There's no electricity, so bring plenty of power banks, a headlamp, and spare batteries.
Bring at least 3 liters of drinking water per person per day. Use the campsite's pump water only for washing.
Shaded spots in the agoho forest fill up fast. Arrive before
10 AM
and you can pick a good spot.
The sand is fine and blows into your tent when the wind picks up. Bring long tent stakes suited for sand and a waterproof ground sheet.
Boat fares are negotiable, but a cheaply contracted boat sometimes fails to keep the return time. Book through a trustworthy resort or a registered boat association.
The rule is to carry out all your trash. Bring several large trash bags.
Winds pick up in the afternoon and waves get higher. Take the return boat before noon if possible, and follow the captain's judgment on days with high waves.
Anawangin's beach drops off steeply, so the water gets deep after just a few steps in. There are no lifeguards, so children and weak swimmers should wear a life vest.
During the wet season and typhoon warnings, the coast guard bans boats from departing. Don't push your way in on an unlicensed boat.
The sand gets very hot at midday, and UV exposure is strong outside the shade. Guard against heatstroke and sunburn.
There have been cases of lost belongings at the campsite. It's best to keep valuables on your person or not bring them at all.
Only build fires and cook in designated areas. The dry agoho forest catches fire easily.
About
1–1.5 hours
by boat from Pundaquit. A wider, quieter volcanic-ash sand beach and agoho forest than Anawangin.

by car. A former U.S. naval base where you can enjoy jungle experiences, a marine theme park, and wreck diving.

by car. A surf beach town in northern Zambales where you can take beginner surf lessons when the waves are good.
